# Pod kill test

Generated from `docs/pod-kill-tests/2026-11-10`.

## What was done

Steady load was driven against `/api/data` through the Service for the whole run. Part
way through, one of the application pods was deleted. The run then continued long enough
for the replacement to start, pass its readiness probe and rejoin the Service.

The delete was an ordinary one, not `--force --grace-period=0`. An ordinary delete is
what a node drain, a rollout and an eviction all do, so it is the case worth testing,
and it is the one that exercises the readiness probe, the preStop pause and graceful
shutdown. A forced delete would skip all three.

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Replicas | 2 |
| Deleted pod | `ratelimitx-877f5cdb-bmdd7` |
| Offered rate | 20.0 req/s |
| Per-user limit (requests/min) | 5,000 |
| Load before the delete | 20.0 s |
| Load after the delete | 60.0 s |
| terminationGracePeriodSeconds | 45 |

## What was measured

A 429 is a correct answer from a rate limiter and is not counted as a failure. Failures
are 5xx responses, statuses the service should never return, and requests that received
no response at all - which is what a dropped connection during a shutdown looks like.

| Measure | Value |
|---------|-------|
| Requests recorded | 1,600 |
| 5xx responses | 0 |
| Requests with no response | 0 |
| Other unexpected statuses | 0 |
| Total failures | 0 (0.0%) |
| Delete issued to pod gone | 16,034 ms |
| Delete issued to a full set of ready endpoints | 15,980 ms |

Both intervals are measured from when the delete was issued, not from when it took
effect, so both are upper bounds. The endpoint figure is also polled once a second, so
it carries up to a second of polling error on top of that.

## By phase

A request belongs to the phase it was *sent* in.

| Phase | What was true | Duration | Requests | 200 | 429 | 5xx | No response | Allowed/s |
|-------|---------------|----------|----------|-----|-----|-----|-------------|-----------|
| before | all replicas ready | 20.1 s | 401 | 401 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 20.0 |
| disruption | a replica missing | 16.0 s | 319 | 319 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 20.0 |
| after | all replicas ready again | 44.0 s | 880 | 880 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 20.0 |

### Response time by phase

Only responses that arrived are included; a request that got none has no service
response time.

| Phase | Responses | p50 | p95 | p99 | max |
|-------|-----------|-----|-----|-----|-----|
| before | 401 | 6 ms | 11 ms | 51 ms | 153 ms |
| disruption | 319 | 5 ms | 10 ms | 1,657 ms | 1,885 ms |
| after | 880 | 6 ms | 11 ms | 539 ms | 1,339 ms |

## Where the requests went

Taken from each pod's own metrics, before and after the run. This is what shows the
Service spread the load instead of sending all of it to one replica - a run that went
entirely to one pod would look identical in every table above.

| Pod | `/api/data` requests served |
|-----|-----------------------------|
| `ratelimitx-877f5cdb-bmdd7` | not measured: deleted during the run, its counter went with it |
| `ratelimitx-877f5cdb-k76fh` | 441 |
| `ratelimitx-877f5cdb-mgzfd` | 963 |

## What this does not show

- **Not a node failure.** The cluster has one node. A pod was deleted; the machine under
  it never went away, and nothing here says what would happen if it did.
- **Not a capacity test.** The remaining replica carried the whole offered rate for the
  duration of the disruption, but that rate was low by design. This says nothing about
  whether one replica could carry production load.
- **One deletion, one run.** The intervals above are a single sample, not a distribution.
- **The load generator shared the machine with the cluster**, so the response times
  include contention a separate generator would not cause.
